answer: On average, original papers in Experimental Economics are markedly longer than original papers in Psychology. In this replication dataset, the mean length of an original paper in Experimental Economics is 28.0 pages (n = 18 unique papers, median 27.5, range 16–45), whereas the mean length of an original paper in Psychology is 11.2 pages (n = 95 unique papers, median 9, range 1–31). That is a difference of about 16.8 pages: economics original papers are roughly 2.5 times longer than psychology original papers. (Excluding the 7 RPP studies flagged for dropping in the source meta-analysis barely changes the Psychology value, to 11.0 pages, and row-level averaging gives 28.0 vs 11.2, so the gap is robust.)

payload.hypothesis: On average, original papers in Experimental Economics are much longer than original papers in Psychology: approximately 28.0 pages (n=18 papers) versus 11.2 pages (n=95 papers), a difference of about 16.8 pages.
payload.workflow: Loaded the main meta-regression CSV (927 rows). Mapped Experimental Economics to project=='ee' and Psychology to project=='rpp' per the data dictionary's project labels (ee≡discipline Economics, AER/QJE; rpp≡Social/Cognitive, PS/JPSP/JEPLMC; ml1/ml3 Many Labs excluded). Reduced to unique original papers by title because length is an original-paper attribute repeated across replication rows (collapsing two RPP rows that are duplicate replications of the same paper). length had 0 missing values, so no imputation. Averaged length per group (mean, median, SD, n) and ran sensitivities: excluding rpp drop==True rows, row-level averaging, broad Psychology including ml1/ml3, and a discipline-based check.
